name: Throwable hierarchy
desc: Every catchable failure is a Throwable. Error is fatal, Exception splits into checked and unchecked branches.
body:
The compiler only forces handling for the checked branch. Error and RuntimeException are unchecked, so a method can throw them without declaring anything. IOException, SQLException, and InterruptedException are checked and must be caught or declared.

When you catch, put the narrowest type first. A catch for Exception before IOException is a compile error because the second clause can never be reached.

name: Checked and unchecked
desc: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared. Unchecked exceptions do not, and usually signal a bug or bad input.
body:
A useful rule: checked exceptions describe failures outside your control, such as a missing file or a refused connection. Unchecked exceptions describe mistakes inside your code, such as a null reference or an index out of range.

Do not turn every checked exception into a RuntimeException just to avoid a signature. Translate only at a layer boundary, and pass the original exception as the cause.

name: try / catch
desc: Runs a block and handles a matching exception instead of letting it leave the method.
body:
The catch block runs only when the exception type matches or is a supertype. After it finishes, execution continues after the whole try statement, not inside the try block where the failure happened.

Keep the try block short. A wide block that catches Exception hides which line failed and makes the handler guess.

name: Multi-catch
desc: Handles several unrelated exception types with one block. The parameter is effectively final.
body:
The alternatives must be unrelated. Writing IOException together with FileNotFoundException does not compile, because the second is a subclass of the first.

The variable type becomes the closest common supertype of the alternatives, so you can call only members that all of them share. Assigning to the parameter is not allowed.

name: finally
desc: Runs cleanup on every exit path: normal end, handled exception, unhandled exception, return, break, or continue.
body:
Use finally for cleanup that has no AutoCloseable form, or for a counter or log line that must always run. When the resource implements AutoCloseable, try-with-resources is the better tool because it keeps the original exception and attaches close failures as suppressed.

System.exit skips finally blocks. A JVM crash or a killed process skips them too.

name: try-with-resources
desc: Closes every AutoCloseable resource at block end, in reverse declaration order, even when the body throws.
body:
Multiple resources close in reverse order. Declare Connection, then PreparedStatement, then ResultSet, and the ResultSet closes first, which is what the database expects.

The resource variable is in scope only inside the try block. A catch clause cannot read it.

name: Suppressed exceptions
desc: When the body throws and close also throws, the body failure stays primary and the close failure is attached as suppressed.
body:
A hand-written finally that calls close would replace the body exception with the close exception, and the real cause would be lost. Try-with-resources avoids that by suppressing instead of replacing.

Call addSuppressed only when you are already handling the primary exception. Adding the primary to itself throws IllegalArgumentException.

name: throw and throws
syntax: throw new Type(message);  /  void m() throws Type
desc: throw raises one exception object. throws declares which checked types may leave the method.
body:
Declaring IllegalArgumentException in a throws clause is legal but pointless, because it is unchecked. Exam answers usually expect throws only for checked types such as IOException or SQLException.

A method can declare a supertype, but then callers cannot catch the narrow type the compiler knows about. Declare the most specific checked types that can actually escape.

name: Custom exception
desc: Defines a failure type the caller can distinguish, optionally carrying fields that the handler needs.
body:
Extend Exception for a recoverable, expected failure. Extend RuntimeException for a programming error or invalid argument that every caller would only rethrow.

Always provide a constructor that takes a cause. Without it, callers wrap the original failure in a new exception and lose the stack trace that explains the root.

name: DriverManager.getConnection()
desc: Opens a physical database connection for a JDBC URL. Close it when the unit of work ends.
body:
Each call returns a new physical connection unless a pool sits behind the driver. Opening one per query is slow and can exhaust the server's connection limit under load.

Credentials belong in the method arguments, not in the URL, because URLs end up in logs and shell history.

name: Driver class and jar
desc: The driver jar must be on the classpath. Modern JDBC loads it through ServiceLoader, so Class.forName is usually unnecessary.
body:
No suitable driver found is a classpath problem, not a SQL problem. Check the jar name, the classpath separator, and the URL prefix in that order.

The JDBC 4 service file inside the jar names the driver class, which is why explicit loading is not required in normal applications.

name: Connection.prepareStatement()
desc: Creates a statement with placeholders. Binding values separately prevents injection and lets the driver handle quoting.
body:
Placeholders stand for values only. A table name, a column name, or ASC and DESC cannot be bound, so build those from a fixed whitelist in Java.

Unbound parameters fail at execute time. The driver message names the missing index, which is usually enough to find the bug.

name: ResultSet.next()
desc: Moves the cursor to the next row and returns false after the last one. The cursor starts before the first row.
body:
Read by label when the query is stable, by index when two columns share a label. Both are 1-based for indexes and case-insensitive in most drivers.

The result set closes when its statement closes, but closing it explicitly returns the cursor to the server sooner.

name: Insert, update, delete
desc: Returns the number of affected rows. Use it to detect a missing row, because a matched-nothing update returns 0.
body:
executeUpdate is for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and DDL. executeQuery is for SELECT. Calling the wrong one throws SQLException with a message about the result type.

A foreign key violation arrives as SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException, a subclass of SQLException. Catch it only when the code can actually recover, such as reporting a duplicate email to the user.

name: commit and rollback
desc: Groups statements into one unit of work. A failure rolls back every statement in the transaction.
body:
MySQL commits DDL implicitly. A CREATE TABLE in the middle of a transaction ends it, so keep schema changes outside the unit of work.

A savepoint rolls back only part of the transaction. Call setSavepoint before the optional step, then rollback(savepoint) on failure and commit the rest.

name: addBatch and executeBatch
desc: Sends many parameter sets in one round trip. The returned array holds one count per statement.
body:
Batch without a transaction still commits row by row in autoCommit mode, which defeats part of the purpose. Disable autoCommit, add every row, execute, then commit once.

MySQL performs better with rewriteBatchedStatements=true in the URL. Keep batches in the hundreds or low thousands; huge batches are hard to retry after a failure.

name: SQL injection
syntax: SELECT ... WHERE city = ?   // never string concatenation
desc: Concatenated input can change the SQL grammar. A placeholder binds the value as data and never as code.
body:
The driver escapes the value and the server parses the SQL before the value arrives, so quotes inside the value cannot become syntax. That is the whole defense.

A prepared query still needs an authorization condition. A user who can pass any customer_email can read another customer's rows if the WHERE clause does not also filter by the logged-in owner.

name: getGeneratedKeys()
desc: Returns auto-increment values created by the statement, without a second query.
body:
Use the key result set instead of SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID(). The second query can run on a different pooled connection and return another session's id.

The key result set has one column in most drivers, so getInt(1) is the portable read. Some drivers also allow the column name.
